What do we mean by reasoning?
DEFINITION  Producing intermediate steps that connect a question to its answer, instead of answering in one shot.
Reasoning, operationally: the intermediate steps a model writes between input and answer.

Why intermediate tokens help
DEFINITION  Each step the model writes becomes input for the next — generated tokens act as working memory.
Theorem · Li, Liu, Zhou & Ma, ICLR 2024
Any problem solvable by a Boolean circuit of size T can be solved by a constant-size transformer that generates O(T) intermediate tokens.
Direct answer: one forward pass
layer 1
layer 2
layer 3
layer 4
depth fixed — computation must fit
With chain-of-thought: computation unrolled
3
8
10
18
24
Example: summing 3, 5, 2, 8, 6 — each token stores the running total and is fed back as input → O(T) serial steps at fixed depth
Caveats: CoT reasoning, not CoT prompting — and an expressivity result, not a guarantee that training finds it.
Source: Li et al., “Chain of Thought Empowers Transformers to Solve Inherently Serial Problems,” ICLR 2024 · Zhou, CS25 (2025)

07 / 36
Chain-of-thought prompting
DEFINITION  Show the model a few worked examples so it writes its own steps before the answer.
One of eight exemplars
Q: Roger has 5 tennis balls. He buys 2 more cans of tennis balls. Each can has 3 tennis balls. How many tennis balls does he have now?
A: Roger started with 5 balls. 2 cans of 3 tennis balls each is 6 tennis balls. 5 + 6 = 11. The answer is 11.
Scale matters
Gains appear only at roughly 100B+ parameters; small models write fluent but wrong chains.

Q: A juggler can juggle 16 balls. Half of the balls are golf balls, and half of the golf balls are blue. How many blue golf balls are there?
A: Let’s think step by step. 16 balls in total; half are golf balls → 8 golf balls; half of those are blue → 4 blue golf balls.

Decompose: least-to-most prompting
DEFINITION  Split a hard problem into easier subproblems, then solve them in order.
Example (Zhou et al., Fig. 1)
It takes Amy 4 minutes to climb to the top of a slide. It takes her 1 minute to slide down. The slide closes in 15 minutes. How many times can she slide before it closes?
① decompose
First ask: “How long does each trip take?”
② solve subproblem
Each trip = 4 + 1 = 5 minutes
③ solve the original
15 ÷ 5 = 3 → she can slide 3 times
SCAN · every split, incl. length
≥99%
vs 16%
least-to-most
CoT
with only 14 exemplars (code-davinci-002); specialised SCAN models train on 15,000+ examples
Analogical prompting
Self-generate related, solved problems first (Yasunaga et al., ICLR 2024).
Step-back prompting
Derive the governing principle first (Zheng et al., ICLR 2024).

CoT decoding: no prompt needed
DEFINITION  Try several decoding branches; keep the one whose answer the model is most confident in.
Q: I have 3 apples, my dad has 2 more apples than me, how many apples do we have in total?
branch on top-k first tokens
greedy · top-1
“5 apples.”
another top-k branch
“… my dad has 3 + 2 = 5 apples. 3 + 5 = 8. We have 8 apples.”
confidence on the answer
low → wrong
high → correct, selected
Confidence = probability gap between the top-1 and top-2 token, averaged over the answer tokens. Selecting by output length is not reliable. Open question: can we make reasoning paths rank first? → RL (Part 2)
Source: Wang & Zhou, “Chain-of-Thought Reasoning Without Prompting,” NeurIPS 2024 · example after Zhou, CS25 (2025)

Self-consistency: sample, then vote
DEFINITION  Sample several reasoning paths and return the answer that appears most often.
CoT prompt
Janet’s ducks lay 16 eggs a day. She eats 3, bakes with 4, sells the rest at $2. Daily revenue?
16 − 3 − 4 = 9 eggs; 9 × $2 → $18
(a flawed path) … → $26
sells 16 − 7 = 9 eggs at $2 → $18
Majority vote
$18
â = argmaxₐ Σᵢ 1[aᵢ = a] ≈ argmaxₐ P(a | q)
Decoding maximizes P(path, answer | q); we want P(answer | q). Voting marginalizes out the reasoning path.

Verifiers: outcome vs process
DEFINITION  A model that scores solutions — on the final answer only (outcome) or step by step (process).
Outcome reward model
Feedback on the final answer only. Cheap: answers can be checked automatically.
Toy: solve 2x + 3 = 11
2x = 8
x = 8 − 2
x = 6 ✗
Knows the answer is wrong — not where.
Process reward model
Feedback on every step. Costly: humans label each step.
Toy: solve 2x + 3 = 11
2x = 8 ✓
x = 8 − 2 ✗
x = 6
Pinpoints the faulty step (should be 8 ÷ 2).

2.6×

Example rationale (Zelikman et al., Fig. 1)
Q: What can be used to carry a small dog? (a) swimming pool (b) basket (c) dog show (d) backyard (e) own home
A: The answer must be able to carry a small dog. Baskets are designed to hold things. So the answer is basket (b).
Filter by correctness, then train — a precursor of RL with verifiable rewards.
Source: Zelikman, Wu, Mu & Goodman, “STaR: Bootstrapping Reasoning With Reasoning,” NeurIPS 2022 (Stanford)

Length bias, and two fixes
DEFINITION  A training objective that accidentally rewards longer answers, even wrong ones.
Dr. GRPO — GRPO done right
Dividing by |oᵢ| spreads a wrong answer’s penalty over its tokens: long wrong answers are penalized less per token, so length grows.
Wrong answer, Â = −1 (illustration)
100 tokens → −0.01 per token
1,000 tokens → −0.001 per token
Fix: drop 1/|oᵢ| and std(r). Better token efficiency; a 7B base model reaches 43.3% on AIME 2024.
DAPO — four techniques
Clip-Higher
avoids entropy collapse
Dynamic sampling
drops prompts whose answers all score alike — e.g. all correct ⇒ Â = 0, no gradient
Token-level loss
essential for long CoT
Overlong shaping
cuts truncation noise

The DeepSeek-R1 training recipe
DEFINITION  Alternate supervised fine-tuning and RL so the reasoning is both strong and readable.
01
Cold-start SFT
V3-Base tuned on a small set of readable long-CoT data
02
Reasoning RL
GRPO on verifiable tasks + language-consistency signal
03
Sample + SFT
rejection-sampled reasoning data plus non-reasoning data
04
General RL
reward models for helpfulness and harmlessness
OUTPUT
DeepSeek-R1
Distillation
Fine-tune smaller dense models on R1’s traces: reasoning without RL on the small model.
Why stages?
Cold start fixes R1-Zero’s readability; the last RL stage restores general helpfulness without losing reasoning.

DEFINITION  Changes that should not matter — reordering facts, adding irrelevant text — still change the answer.
Premise order

in proof order
If A then B

shuffled — same logic

>30%

Best when premises follow the proof. R-GSM: a reordered GSM8K.
Irrelevant context
Shi et al. · ICML 2023
Constructed example, in the style of GSM-IC
Jan has 3 boxes with 4 pens in each.
Her brother is 12 years old.
How many pens does Jan have?

RL-trained
base (dashed)

Can we trust the chain-of-thought?
DEFINITION  Whether the written chain of thought reflects the real reason for the model’s answer.
Unfaithful explanations · Turpin et al., NeurIPS 2023
prompt with bias: answers always “(A)”
CoT never mentions the bias
answer (A)
max accuracy drop, 13 BIG-Bench Hard tasks (GPT-3.5, Claude 1.0)
Intrinsic self-correction · Huang et al., ICLR 2024
answer
“review your answer”
often no better, sometimes worse
Without external feedback LLMs struggle to self-correct reasoning. Feedback that works comes from outside: tests, solvers, verifiers.
Treat a chain-of-thought as useful computation and weak evidence — not as a faithful account of why the model answered.
